title: Taking amrit
hook: the initiation, given by five Sikhs, is a serious personal step, never pressed on anyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, kurehat: the four things an initiated Sikh avoids. Your line was keep it clean. Did one clean habit hold for the day? Today, the ceremony where that promise is made. Day two hundred seventy-one.

Think of the biggest promise you've ever made on purpose. Not a quick yes in a group chat. The kind you thought about for weeks, maybe years, and then said out loud in front of people who mattered. A wedding vow. Signing up for something hard. For many Sikhs there's a promise like that, and it happens in a quiet room, in front of five people, with a steel bowl of sweetened water. Nobody can sign you up for it. Nobody is supposed to push you into it. Today: taking amrit.
screen: `THE BIGGEST PROMISE YOU'VE MADE.` → `FIVE PEOPLE, ONE STEEL BOWL.` → `NOBODY SIGNS YOU UP.`

segments.voice: Amrit means the nectar of immortality. Sanchar means bringing it into being, passing it on. Together, amrit sanchar is the Sikh initiation, also called khande di pahul, the initiation of the double-edged sword. It goes back to Vaisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur. Guru Gobind Singh stirred water in an iron bowl with a khanda, a double-edged sword. Tradition says Mata Sahib Kaur added sugar puffs, so the steel would carry sweetness too. He gave it to the first five, the panj pyare, the five beloved ones. And then he did something surprising. He asked the five to give it to him. The Guru, with folded hands, received it from the people he had just initiated. The ceremony today keeps that shape. Five initiated Sikhs, standing in for the panj pyare, prepare the amrit while reciting five prayers from the Sikh daily prayers, including Guru Nanak's Japji. The person taking it drinks from cupped hands, and it's sprinkled on the eyes and the hair. They greet each other: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. The Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory. They're taught the code: the five Ks, the daily prayers, and the four things avoided that we met yesterday. So this is a real commitment, and Sikhs treat it that way. People take amrit at different ages: some as teenagers, some in their forties, some never. The Sikh code of conduct says anyone of any background who is ready to live by the vows may take it. The word that matters is ready. Amrit isn't handed out to fill a room. It's a step a person chooses when the promise is theirs.
screen: `AMRIT — THE NECTAR OF IMMORTALITY.` · `ANANDPUR, 1699: THE FIRST FIVE.` · `THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE TO INITIATE HIM.` · `A STEP TAKEN WHEN YOU'RE READY.` · then, large: `A STEP, NOT A PRESSURE.`

segments.voice: Think of one commitment in your own life, one you made, or one you're still weighing. Ask it three honest questions. Is this mine, or am I doing it because someone expects it? What would it ask of me on an ordinary Tuesday? And what would keeping it give back? You don't have to decide anything now. Just let the questions sit, the way the five let the water be stirred slowly. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Amrit sanchar. The Sikh initiation, given by five initiated Sikhs, with water stirred by a double-edged sword. A serious step, chosen, never pressed.
Your line: a step, not a pressure. Today, when you ask someone for a yes, leave them room to say not yet. Day two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Amrit sanchar is held in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, usually in a gurdwara, where five initiated Sikhs prepare amrit in an iron bowl while reciting five banis; those who take it commit to the five Ks, daily prayer and the Rehat.

fork.setup: Anandpur, 1699. you're the Guru. you've just initiated the first five. what next?
options: stand above them as their commander.
ask the five to give amrit to you.
send them home and close the ceremony.
fork.reveal: tradition says Guru Gobind Singh asked the five to initiate him. the teacher took the step his students took.

original.note: Gurmukhi: amrit, the nectar of immortality; sanchar, bringing it into being and passing it on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a kind of baptism every Sikh child gets.
what it means: a chosen initiation, given by five initiated Sikhs, taken when a person is ready to keep the vows.
what a scholar hears: amrit is the old Indic word for the drink of deathlessness (a-mrit, not-dead); the rite is also called khande di pahul, and its form goes back to Vaisakhi 1699.

notes: Confirm the five banis recited during preparation (Japji, Jaap, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand Sahib) and that saying 'including Guru Nanak's Japji' is accurate for all practice.
Mata Sahib Kaur adding patashe (sugar puffs) is tradition; confirm the framing.
The Rehat Maryada wording on who may take amrit (any person, of any country, religion or caste, who is ready to abide by the vows) is paraphrased; confirm.
'Sanchar' glossed as bringing into being and passing on; confirm the gloss.
Reviewer softened 'the Guru knelt' to 'with folded hands'; the posture is tradition, not recorded detail. Confirm the preferred telling.
